{"answer": "# Metal-powder atomizer collectors: reported failures and applicable guidance

**Finding.** I did not locate a verifiable report of an AMAZEMET rePOWDER—or another metal-powder atomizer—in which hot shot or molten runoff **burned a powder-collector seal, cracked a glass collection vessel, or caused a measured oxygen rise through a damaged collector seal**. The sources below document related failures and preventive designs, but do not establish those particular event–cause–fix chains. They should not be cited as proof that such a collector incident occurred. (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000032, pqac-00000034, pqac-00000045)

The distinction between an observed failure and a design precaution is consequential here:

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

The clearest nearby failure is the Savannah River Pd-alloy gas-atomization run: erroneous thermocouple readings drove excessive heating, alumina parts fractured, and a broken stopper **blocked** the nozzle. The metal therefore did **not** run into the collector; the reported change was to noncontact infrared pyrometry. The paper’s equipment schematic shows the cooling path and downstream cyclone/collector, but does not depict collector damage. (pqac-00000032, pqac-00000033, pqac-00000047)

In Pratt & Whitney’s centrifugal atomizer, the reported disk-drive **oil-seal** leakage must not be mistaken for a leaking powder-collector gasket. Unstable disk-rim operation produced large splats and could clog the outlet; the report calls for shutdown in that condition and describes lower-head blowdown to move retained powder toward the collector. It does not identify a repair for the oil seals. Howmet’s Spraycast-X account likewise reports special seals installed *to avoid* chamber leakage and better cleanliness at low leak-up, without identifying a thermally damaged collector seal. (pqac-00000034, pqac-00000035)

## Choosing the hot-side collector, seals and glass

**Separate melt temperature from seal temperature.** For a melt above 1,000 °C, the relevant elastomer limit is the *measured or conservatively predicted temperature at its installed sealing surface*, including credible upset conditions—not the nominal melt temperature or a material name alone. Seal guidance warns that formulation, chemistry, swelling, thermal expansion and gland design all matter; FKM grades are not interchangeable, and even FFKM must be selected by grade and service. A cited mechanical-seal review describes ordinary FKM service around 400 °F (approximately 204 °C), with some specialty *static* compounds rated to 250 °F (approximately 121 °C); these are **not** ratings for direct contact with molten metal. That review is not a collector qualification standard. (pqac-00000041, pqac-00000042)

**Keep the impact and runoff path metallic and away from elastomers.** The LLNL/Arcast atomizer specification calls for a stainless-steel vacuum chamber, a lower cone, isolation valves and six explosion-rated removable powder hoppers; EURECAT describes a sloped metal lower cone leading to its collector. A separate high-temperature vacuum reactor demonstrates water cooling of a flange and use of Viton seals at *cooled* quartz windows, not at the hot workpiece. Accordingly, a metal receiving pot or catch tray, a shielded or cooled collector flange, and a seal outside any direct shot/runoff path are defensible **design recommendations** to assess and validate—not fixes shown to have followed a collector fire in these publications. Verify their thermal performance and the collector’s pressure/vacuum rating for the actual installation. (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000040, pqac-00000045)

**Do not substitute an ordinary glass jar for a qualified hot-metal receiver.** In an optical-access high-temperature apparatus, the designers rejected soda-lime and borosilicate glass and selected quartz for its lower thermal expansion and higher continuous operating-temperature capability; they also cushioned and sealed its metal interfaces with gaskets and sized the window for the applicable pressure difference. Comparative glass data give approximate expansion coefficients of 3.4 × 10⁻⁶/°C for borosilicate and 0.55 × 10⁻⁶/°C for fused silica. These properties favor an engineered, protected observation window where optical access is necessary; **neither source certifies quartz or borosilicate as a vessel safe from direct molten-metal impact**. Window strength, mounting stress, thermal gradients and pressure loading still require specific engineering assessment. (pqac-00000036, pqac-00000039)

A conservative operating rule is to **stop the melt/atomization sequence and retain the inert atmosphere** if visible runoff, abnormally coarse shot, collector or flange overheating, smoke, glass damage, loss of cooling, a seal leak, or unexplained oxygen rise occurs; keep the collector isolated until the equipment is safe to inspect. This is a proposed stop rule inferred from the documented blocked-outlet/shutdown experience and containment designs, **not** a manufacturer-prescribed rePOWDER procedure. (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000034)

## Checking chamber integrity

For a *clean, dry, assembled* chamber—including its collector joints—evacuate, isolate the pump and record pressure against time. The measured gas load is **Q = V(dP/dt)** and contains both leakage and outgassing; a nearly linear sustained rise favors a real leak, whereas a rise that progressively levels off can indicate outgassing/re-adsorption. This test alone does not locate a faulty seal, and a dirty or recently heated chamber can confound it. The published pressure-rise comparison illustrates that distinction. (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021, pqac-00000037, pqac-00000048)

Locate suspect collector flanges and other joints with an appropriately configured **helium leak detector** while applying helium locally. A published large-vessel investigation enclosed individual flange gaps and welds, introduced helium to each enclosure, corrected detector readings for gas diverted through parallel pumping, retightened leaking flanges and re-welded a defective port. Its illustrated enclosure method is useful, but its numerical joint acceptance threshold is specific to that facility. The LLNL/Arcast *atomizer design specification* instead states a whole-system leak requirement of **less than 1 × 10⁻⁶ atm·cm³/s**; the specification does not itself demonstrate that a particular machine passed testing. Set acceptance criteria and test configuration for the actual atomizer rather than transferring either example uncritically. (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000019, pqac-00000022, pqac-00000038, pqac-00000049)

**No retrieved rePOWDER instruction specifies an automatic post-outage sensor check.** As a documented *analyzer-manual analogy*, the GPR-3100B oxygen analyzer performs power-on diagnostics; its manual describes allowing stabilization and calibration after installation, flushing the selected sample/calibration gas before reading, and ensuring that calibration-gas pressure and temperature are representative of the sample. Its power-failure alarm opens when power is lost. These instructions should not be represented as AMAZEMET settings or as proof that every brief outage invalidates calibration. (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000027, pqac-00000028)

Before relying on a restarted chamber reading to authorize a new melt, an appropriate **proposed verification** is to confirm analyzer self-test, sample flow and sampling-line integrity; check a low-oxygen reference and a suitable independent span or functional challenge under the installed analyzer manufacturer’s procedure; confirm that alarm and interlock states have returned correctly; and independently confirm chamber pressure integrity and oxygen stability after purge. Do not accept an apparently low displayed oxygen value by itself as evidence that a collector seal is sound. The available oxygen-analyzer manual supports stabilization, controlled sample presentation, zero/span calibration and attention to the power-failure alarm; the LLNL atomizer specification supports redundant oxygen monitoring, but neither supplies a universal atomizer-specific outage acceptance threshold. (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000025, pqac-00000028, pqac-00000030)"}

A separate high-temperature vacuum reactor demonstrates water cooling of a flange and use of Viton seals at *cooled* quartz windows, not at the hot workpiece. Accordingly, a metal receiving pot or catch tray, a shielded or cooled collector flange, and a seal outside any direct shot/runoff path are defensible **design recommendations** to assess and validate—not fixes shown to have followed a collector fire in these publications. Verify their thermal performance and the collector’s pressure/vacuum rating for the actual installation. (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000040, pqac-00000045)

**Do not substitute an ordinary glass jar for a qualified hot-metal receiver.** In an optical-access high-temperature apparatus, the designers rejected soda-lime and borosilicate glass and selected quartz for its lower thermal expansion and higher continuous operating-temperature capability; they also cushioned and sealed its metal interfaces with gaskets and sized the window for the applicable pressure difference. Comparative glass data give approximate expansion coefficients of 3.4 × 10⁻⁶/°C for borosilicate and 0.55 × 10⁻⁶/°C for fused silica. These properties favor an engineered, protected observation window where optical access is necessary; **neither source certifies quartz or borosilicate as a vessel safe from direct molten-metal impact**. Window strength, mounting stress, thermal gradients and pressure loading still require specific engineering assessment. (pqac-00000036, pqac-00000039)

A conservative operating rule is to **stop the melt/atomization sequence and retain the inert atmosphere** if visible runoff, abnormally coarse shot, collector or flange overheating, smoke, glass damage, loss of cooling, a seal leak, or unexplained oxygen rise occurs; keep the collector isolated until the equipment is safe to inspect. This is a proposed stop rule inferred from the documented blocked-outlet/shutdown experience and containment designs, **not** a manufacturer-prescribed rePOWDER procedure. (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000034)

## Checking chamber integrity

For a *clean, dry, assembled* chamber—including its collector joints—evacuate, isolate the pump and record pressure against time. The measured gas load is **Q = V(dP/dt)** and contains both leakage and outgassing; a nearly linear sustained rise favors a real leak, whereas a rise that progressively levels off can indicate outgassing/re-adsorption. This test alone does not locate a faulty seal, and a dirty or recently heated chamber can confound it. The published pressure-rise comparison illustrates that distinction. (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021, pqac-00000037, pqac-00000048)

Locate suspect collector flanges and other joints with an appropriately configured **helium leak detector** while applying helium locally. A published large-vessel investigation enclosed individual flange gaps and welds, introduced helium to each enclosure, corrected detector readings for gas diverted through parallel pumping, retightened leaking flanges and re-welded a defective port. Its illustrated enclosure method is useful, but its numerical joint acceptance threshold is specific to that facility. The LLNL/Arcast *atomizer design specification* instead states a whole-system leak requirement of **less than 1 × 10⁻⁶ atm·cm³/s**; the specification does not itself demonstrate that a particular machine passed testing. Set acceptance criteria and test configuration for the actual atomizer rather than transferring either example uncritically. (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000019, pqac-00000022, pqac-00000038, pqac-00000049)

## Trace-oxygen indication following loss of power

**No retrieved rePOWDER instruction specifies an automatic post-outage sensor check.** As a documented *analyzer-manual analogy*, the GPR-3100B oxygen analyzer performs power-on diagnostics; its manual describes allowing stabilization and calibration after installation, flushing the selected sample/calibration gas before reading, and ensuring that calibration-gas pressure and temperature are representative of the sample. Its power-failure alarm opens when power is lost. These instructions should not be represented as AMAZEMET settings or as proof that every brief outage invalidates calibration. (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000027, pqac-00000028)

Before relying on a restarted chamber reading to authorize a new melt, an appropriate **proposed verification** is to confirm analyzer self-test, sample flow and sampling-line integrity; check a low-oxygen reference and a suitable independent span or functional challenge under the installed analyzer manufacturer’s procedure; confirm that alarm and interlock states have returned correctly; and independently confirm chamber pressure integrity and oxygen stability after purge. Do not accept an apparently low displayed oxygen value by itself as evidence that a collector seal is sound. The available oxygen-analyzer manual supports stabilization, controlled sample presentation, zero/span calibration and attention to the power-failure alarm; the LLNL atomizer specification supports redundant oxygen monitoring, but neither supplies a universal atomizer-specific outage acceptance threshold. (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000025, pqac-00000028, pqac-00000030)

contexts.context: The excerpt does not report whether material spilled or reached a collector, glass jar, seal, or gasket, and it does not mention the rePOWDER apparatus specifically. It does, however, identify several ultrasonic-atomizer design and operational limitations. The ATO system requires management of thermal fatigue at the sonotrode’s hot end, stabilization of the sonotrode temperature through liquid cooling, and sufficiently low damping of ultrasonic vibrations. The authors also note a risk of high-cycle fatigue. Droplet transport must be given enough initial kinetic energy to prevent particles from striking internal atomization-chamber surfaces, since such impacts would cause powder loss and reduce raw-material utilization. Ultrasonic power must overcome surface tension and viscosity, with higher power required at lower atomization temperatures because larger droplets and higher resistance are produced. The reported design remedy is a cooled sonotrode with liquid cooling on non-working surfaces, together with appropriate sizing of ultrasonic power and control of atomization frequency and temperature. These points concern process containment, efficiency, and equipment durability, but they do not establish any observed spill or contact with a collector, jar, seal, or gasket.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports a gas-spray atomization failure caused by progressively divergent and faulty C-type thermocouple readings. The erroneous readings allowed the melt temperature to exceed the functional temperature range of the alumina components, resulting in failure of multiple ceramic parts and loss of the Pd-alloy charge. After the stopper rod was raised repeatedly, no metal exited the nozzle, although personnel confirmed that the stopper mechanism moved. Post-run inspection found ceramic material floating on the solidified melt, thermocouple sheath ends displaced and frozen at the surface, and substantial stopper-rod damage. X-ray and CT imaging showed a break across the stopper rod diameter, with a large ceramic section missing and liquid metal occupying the void; another ceramic loss was possible on the opposite side. The equipment configuration included a zirconia crucible, densified-alumina stopper rod, alumina thermocouple tubes, zirconia lids, and a steel vacuum chamber. contexts.context: The excerpt reports a thermally induced failure in the gas-spray atomization crucible system during processing of a Pd alloy. Thermocouple readings became erroneous, causing operators to apply excessive RF heating power; the lower temperature reading was incorrectly used as the melt temperature. The estimated liquid-metal temperature reached approximately 1,918 °C, near the alumina melting point, causing loss of ceramic structural integrity. The ceramic stopper rod fractured, and both thin-walled alumina thermocouple over-sheaths also failed and floated in the melt. The failure was exacerbated by the stopper rod’s mechanical loading: a spring applied approximately 25.5 psi, while a 1–3 mm alignment offset created a bending moment; creep rupture after the metal became liquid was hypothesized. The broken lower stopper-rod section remained lodged in the nozzle throat, blocking liquid-metal flow, although the upper assembly could be removed. The implemented change was replacement of contact thermocouples with non-contact infrared optical pyrometry to improve temperature measurement and avoid recurrence. This excerpt does not report failures involving a leaking atmosphere, cracked glass, or burnt seals, nor does it identify corresponding causes or corrective changes for those equipment issues.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes the principal gas-atomization and vacuum-system modifications made for Spraycast-X, but it does not provide specific details about seal designs, evacuation procedures, leak-up rates, or measured leakage problems. Because aerospace customers were concerned about nonmetallic inclusions, Howmet modified the Osprey approach so that melting and gas atomization were performed under vacuum and with high-purity inert gas. Howmet combined its existing vacuum-casting experience with knowledge obtained from Osprey Metals to design a pilot facility. The resulting process used vacuum induction melting followed by atomization with high-purity argon, rather than simply using an exposed or less-controlled atomization environment. The equipment was arranged as two water-cooled chambers: an upper vacuum melting chamber containing the induction furnace, atomizer, and tundish, and a lower chamber containing the deposition collector and programmable motion system. The excerpt states that the system could process up to 650 lb of superalloy at deposition rates up to 100 lb/min and accommodate a rotating mandrel as large as 33 inches in diameter by 20 inches long. Thus, the available text supports discussion of vacuum/high-purity-gas cleanliness objectives and the two-chamber facility modification, but not the requested specific seal, pump-down, leak-up, or troubleshooting information.

contexts.context: The report identifies atmosphere control and chamber leakage as important gas-atomization/process issues. The system was first evacuated and then backfilled with argon; special seal designs were added specifically to prevent leakage during operation. Subsequent EB-button melting and metallographic evaluations showed that maintaining a tight vacuum and very low chamber leak-up rates reduced undesirable oxide and nitride inclusions in the spray-cast product, potentially achieving cleanliness comparable to the starting ingot. The excerpt does not specify the detailed mechanical design of the seal modifications, but it explicitly records the installation of special seals and the operational emphasis on evacuation, leak prevention, and low leak-up conditions. Gas choice also affected contamination: argon processing generally produced less than 15 ppm oxygen and nitrogen pickup, whereas nitrogen atomization led to substantially higher residual nitrogen in the deposits, reported as 124–564 ppm. Thus, the practical modifications described were evacuation before argon backfill, improved sealing, and operation under tighter vacuum/controlled leak-up conditions.

contexts.context: The excerpt identifies atomizing-gas pressure and gas type as important Spraycast-X process variables affecting the deposit. Grain size increased at lower atomizing-gas pressures, while higher metal flow rates also produced larger grains. Because argon has approximately half the heat capacity of nitrogen, argon atomization generally generated a hotter spray-cast deposit and consequently a larger grain size. The passage also indicates that atomizing-gas pressure was a critical parameter for both billet and ring-preform products. However, this excerpt does not describe specific gas-atomization problems involving seals, evacuation procedures, leak-up testing, or actual equipment modifications. It mentions other ring-preform variables—mandrel diameter and reciprocating speed—as critical, while superheat, rotational speed, and atomizer frequency generally had only minor effects depending on the product. contexts.context: The article documents a pump-isolation, rate-of-rise method for measuring gas throughput. After the chamber reaches an equilibrium pressure with pumping active, the pump or high-vacuum valve is isolated and chamber pressure is recorded versus time. For a chamber of constant volume, throughput is calculated from Q = d(pV)/dt = V dp/dt; the slope of a linear pressure-versus-time trace is Q/V. The method is applied both to intentional real leaks, produced by opening a calibrated needle valve, and to virtual leaks or outgassing, where pressure rises toward an equilibrium after isolation. Outgassing from samples is estimated from the post-isolation pressure-rise rate, while the empty chamber provides a background outgassing baseline. The excerpt notes that samples were pumped for half an hour and that pressure-rise curves were recorded for background, Viton, and Teflon samples. It does not provide a specific water-outgassing diagnostic, helium-spray procedure, or documented method for locating a leak with helium spray. It does, however, distinguish real leaks from virtual leaks operationally: a real leak is associated with a fixed gas throughput through the needle valve during pumping, whereas a virtual leak/outgassing source produces a pressure rise after isolation.

contexts.context: The excerpt documents a rate-of-rise (pressure-buildup) test in which the chamber was evacuated to 2 × 10−6 mbar using a dry screw pump, booster, and two turbo-molecular pumps. The valve was then closed to isolate the pumps, and the pressure increase was monitored with pressure gauges. With pumping stopped (S = 0), the total gas load is calculated from Q—or qtotal—= V dP/dt, and is treated as the sum of outgassing and leakage: qtotal = qoutgassing + qleak. The paper explicitly considers two diagnostic limiting cases: if outgassing dominates, the pressure-rise behavior is modeled using a decaying outgassing rate and re-adsorption pumping; if leakage dominates, the pressure rise directly approximates qleak. contexts.context: The excerpt documents helium leak-testing methods and a subsequent pressure-related analysis, but it does not explicitly state the rate-of-rise equation Q = V dp/dt or provide a detailed procedure for distinguishing water outgassing from a real leak by pump-isolate monitoring. For leak localization, chamber flanges sealed with copper gaskets were individually checked by enveloping the flange gaps with vinyl tape and injecting helium through a needle. Welding lines between the chamber and its ports were tested by enclosing them in a vinyl hood and injecting helium into the hood. The helium detector read leak rates in units of 10−9 mbar·L/s. Values above 0.5 × 10−9 mbar·L/s triggered inspection and adjustment of flange fastening; the highest leaking location was port #47, whose defective weld was removed and re-welded. The article calculates an effective helium distribution ratio of approximately 200:1 between the forepump and detector. Assuming 100 joints and a maximum accepted individual reading of 0.5 × 10−9 mbar·L/s, it estimates a total leak rate of 1 × 10−5 mbar·L/s. Figures are identified as showing the pumping-down curve and pressure-buildup analysis, but the excerpt does not explain how those plots separate water outgassing from leakage.

contexts.context: The excerpt documents a pump-isolate pressure-rise (rate-of-rise) test in which chamber pressure was monitored after isolation and the gas load inferred from the pressure slope. For a leak-dominated load, it gives the relationship V(dP/dt) ≅ q_leak, where V is chamber volume and q_leak is the leak gas load. The observed pressure rise was measured for 110 hours, with an average gas load of 3 × 10−3 mbar·L/s. The article distinguishes outgassing from leakage by curve shape: when outgassing dominates, outgassing and reabsorption rates become similar and the pressure-rise curve gradually converges; when leakage dominates, the curve increases nearly linearly. Residual-gas analysis also found relatively high proportions of N, N2, O2, Ar, and CO2, supporting a significant air-leak problem, although the excerpt does not specifically identify water outgassing. For leak localization, the chamber was evacuated to approximately 10−6 mbar, welding lines and flanges were isolated beneath vinyl hoods and tape, and helium was sprayed/admitted locally to each enclosed section. A helium leak detector connected to the TMP foreline verified individual joint leak rates. The authors caution that measured rates require correction for parallel pumping and line conductance.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides general thermal-expansion guidance relevant to selecting seals for heated equipment, but it does not report specific published service temperatures or thermal-shock limits for vacuum-furnace windows, graphite, elastomers, borosilicate glass, quartz glass, or flange temperature. It explains that seal materials with similar coefficients of thermal expansion (COTE) maintain fits more reliably during temperature changes. Conversely, substantially different COTEs can cause fit changes that result in hang-up, distortion, leakage, or fractures—risks relevant to thermal shock and differential heating between a window, seal, and flange. Common metals are stated to have COTEs of approximately 6 × 10^-6 to 9 × 10^-6 in/in °F, while carbon and ceramic seal faces are approximately 3 × 10^-6 to 4 × 10^-6 in/in °F. Secondary seals may compensate for some differential expansion, but shrink-fit or interference-fit designs depend on initial interference, component size, differential COTE, and temperature increase. The article recommends low-expansion alloys for high-temperature interference fits, while warning that such alloys may perform poorly in corrosive environments. It also emphasizes that API 682 material selections must be checked against proven field experience for each specific application.

contexts.context: A gas-spray atomization Pd-alloy trial reported severe thermal-control failure. Erroneous thermocouple readings caused excessive RF heating; estimated liquid temperature reached ~1,918–2,060°C, near alumina’s 2,072°C melting point. Two alumina TC sheaths and the ceramic stopper rod fractured and floated in the melt. A remaining rod fragment blocked the nozzle, preventing metal discharge; the upper assembly could be removed without opening the nozzle. Spring loading (~25.5 psi) and 1–3 mm misalignment likely promoted creep rupture. The proposed fix was replacing contact thermocouples with infrared optical pyrometry and improving real-time power monitoring.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes helium leak testing of a dirty thermal-vacuum chamber, not powder-atomizer thermal incidents. Chamber flanges used copper gaskets; gaps and welds were covered with vinyl and helium-injected. A helium detector measured \(10^{-9}\) mbar·L/s; joints above \(0.5\times10^{-9}\) were tightened, while defective port #47 was ground out and rewelded. Calculated effective pumping speeds were 65.4 L/s (forepump) and 0.358 L/s (detector), a 200:1 distribution ratio. For 100 joints, estimated total leakage was \(1\times10^{-5}\) mbar·L/s.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes a 100 m³, 304-stainless-steel dirty thermal-vacuum chamber, not a powder atomizer. A 110-hour pressure-buildup test measured an average gas load of \(3\times10^{-3}\) mbar·L/s; the nearly linear pressure rise indicated leakage rather than outgassing. Residual-gas analysis showed relatively high N, N₂, O₂, Ar and CO₂. Investigators therefore performed precision helium leak testing: the chamber was evacuated to ~\(10^{-6}\) mbar, welds/flanges were locally hooded and sealed, and helium was applied externally. The excerpt cautions that parallel TMP pumping caused the detector to under-report actual leak rates.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides background on high-temperature metallic mechanical-seal components, particularly welded metal bellows, but does not give explicit operating-temperature ranges for elastomer vacuum seals such as Viton FKM or silicone. It also does not discuss a metal collector or cooling of a flange in high-temperature apparatus. Welded metal bellows are described as serving simultaneously as a spring, drive, and secondary seal; their thin diaphragms are welded into an accordion-like structure and must flex axially while remaining torsionally rigid. Material selection is challenging because of thin cross sections, welding, cold working or heat treatment, and the need for adequate tensile strength. Alloy 718 is identified as the standard material for welded bellows in high-temperature hydrocarbon processing because it combines corrosion resistance with high-temperature properties that do not significantly degrade over typical mechanical-seal temperatures. Alloy 350 remains suitable for less aggressive environments but has limited corrosion resistance and uncertain compatibility data. Alloy 400 offers corrosion resistance, including in hydrofluoric-acid service, and is used for both metal parts and welded bellows. The excerpt therefore supports general cautions about matching metallic bellows materials to temperature, chemical aggressiveness, welding, and heat treatment, but it lacks the requested explicit elastomer limits or flange-cooling guidance.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not provide explicit material temperature ranges for elastomer vacuum seals, Viton/FKM, silicone, metal seals, metal collectors, or flange-cooling requirements in high-temperature apparatus. It gives general selection cautions that are relevant to such an assessment. Secondary seals are commonly elastomeric and must contain pressure, resist all process chemicals without degradation or swelling, accommodate surface-finish and differential thermal-expansion requirements, and survive installation without damage. Chemical compatibility ratings are only general categories; compatibility must be confirmed for the specific material, grade, chemicals, and operating conditions. For fluoroelastomers (FKMs, including Viton-type materials), higher fluorine content generally improves chemical compatibility, but curing process and other formulation factors substantially affect physical properties, operating temperature, and chemical resistance. The excerpt specifically warns that not all FKMs are equivalent. It also states that material selection depends on process conditions, seal design, tribological properties, and economics, and that no single material is superior in every application. No information is supplied here about silicone temperature limits, metallic seal or collector operating ranges, vacuum-specific elastomer limits, or methods for cooling a flange in a high-temperature setup; those details would need to be obtained from another source or the manufacturer’s grade-specific data.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides temperature limits and application cautions for several elastomers, but it does not specifically discuss vacuum seals, silicone seal temperature ranges, metal seals, metal collectors, or cooling a flange in high-temperature apparatus. Fluoroelastomers (FKM, commonly associated with Viton) are identified as the standard material for many process-industry mechanical seals and are generally preferred for hydrocarbon service at temperatures up to 400°F. However, FKM is not recommended for ketones, amines, low-molecular-weight ethers, esters, hot water, or steam, and is generally not recommended below 215°F; some specialty compounds are rated to 250°F in static applications. EPR/EPDM is presented as a preferred option for hot water and steam up to 400°F, and is also used with silicone-based products, ketones, and alcohols, though contamination by hydrocarbons must be avoided because petroleum oils can cause swelling and seal failure. FFKM is intended for very high temperatures and aggressive chemicals, but grades vary substantially and require careful selection. Most FFKM grades should not be used below 20°F because the material hardens. The excerpt also notes that FFKM has higher thermal expansion than FKM, requiring appropriate groove sizing.

Thermal expansion differences between metal components and seal faces can cause changes in fit, hang-up, distortion, leaks, or fractures; low-expansion alloys are therefore used for high-temperature interference-fit applications. The excerpt states that special alloys may be needed to balance thermal-expansion requirements with corrosion resistance. It also notes that API 682 provides standard material selections and application guidance, but that the standard is not a substitute for field experience, particularly because chemical-processing applications involve varied chemicals, pressures, temperatures, and concentrations. answer.formatted_answer:
Question: Find reports, manuals, application notes or papers on metal powder atomizers (ultrasonic such as the
AMAZEMET rePOWDER, gas, or centrifugal) and other inert-gas melting equipment in which hot metal,
coarse shot or molten runoff reached the powder collection container or its seals, so that elastomer
seals or gaskets overheated, smoked or burned, glass collection vessels or view ports cracked from
thermal shock, or the atmosphere's oxygen rose because a collector seal leaked. For each give the
equipment, what happened, the cause found and the fix (for example seal material, heat shields,
cooled flanges, metal collection pots, catch trays, interlocks or stop rules). Also report published
guidance on choosing seals and glass for powder collectors under melts above 1000 C, on leak testing
(rate of rise, helium) of atomizer chambers, and on how trace-oxygen sensors on such chambers should
be checked after a power failure.


No. # Metal-powder atomizer collectors: reported failures and applicable guidance

**Finding.** I did not locate a verifiable report of an AMAZEMET rePOWDER—or another metal-powder atomizer—in which hot shot or molten runoff **burned a powder-collector seal, cracked a glass collection vessel, or caused a measured oxygen rise through a damaged collector seal**. The sources below document related failures and preventive designs, but do not establish those particular event–cause–fix chains. They should not be cited as proof that such a collector incident occurred. (scientific2023comparisonofultrasonic pages 7-8, [name redacted]2020failureanalysisof pages 1-4, andrus1989thrustchambermaterial pages 88-91, salges2024processingandcharacterization pages 46-50)

The distinction between an observed failure and a design precaution is consequential here:

| Evidence class | Equipment/source | What happened or design provision | Cause/findings | Fix or safeguard actually reported | Relevance to requested collector event |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Documented incident** | SRNL Powder Production Facility, helium gas-spray atomizer, approximately 2.1 kg Pd-alloy charge | Faulty, diverging thermocouple readings prompted excessive RF power. Alumina thermocouple sheaths and the stopper rod failed; the broken rod remained in the nozzle throat and blocked discharge. | Melt temperature was estimated near 1,918–2,060 °C, approaching alumina’s melting point; spring load and slight misalignment probably contributed to creep rupture. | Replace contact thermocouples with non-contact infrared optical pyrometry. The source does **not** report that metal reached or damaged the collector. ([name redacted]2020failureanalysisof pages 1-4, [name redacted]2020failureanalysisof pages 4-10) | Adjacent atomizer overheating failure, **not** a collector-seal or glass-vessel incident. |
| **Documented operating problems** | Pratt & Whitney rapid-solidification-rate centrifugal atomizer | Disk-drive oil seals leaked; unstable rim atomization produced large splats that reduced yield or clogged the outlet. Fine powder and detached wall deposits could obstruct flow to the collector can. | Soft copper adhered to chamber walls; deposits could later fall, while unstable atomization and splashing generated coarse material. The oil-seal leak cause was not reported. | Shutdown was required for unstable atomization; lower-head blowdown nozzles were used to assure powder flow. **No oil-seal repair was specified**, so none should be inferred. (andrus1989thrustchambermaterial pages 88-91) | Closest documented case involving coarse splats and collector-path blockage, but no burned collector gasket, cracked glass, or oxygen rise. |
| **Reported modification, not a collector incident** | Howmet Spraycast-X vacuum-induction melting and gas-atomization system | Special seal designs were installed to avoid operational leakage after evacuation and argon backfill; low leak-up improved product cleanliness. | High chamber leak-up admitted contaminants and increased oxide and nitride inclusions; very low leak-up limited oxygen and nitrogen pickup during argon processing to generally under 15 ppm. | Improved sealing, evacuation before argon backfill, and operation under tight-vacuum and very-low-leak-up conditions. Collector seals were not identified. (prichard1992spraycastx"superalloyfor pages 4-6) | Documents atmosphere-leakage control, **not** hot metal overheating a collector seal. |
| **Preventive specification only** | 2017 LLNL/Arcast free-fall gas atomizer | Stainless-steel high-vacuum chamber; lower cone and six explosion-rated powder-removal hoppers with isolation valves and quick clamps; three redundant paramagnetic oxygen analyzers; specified leak rate below 1 × 10⁻⁶ atm·cm³/s. | Design requirements anticipated reactive, refractory, and radioactive powders and required inert transfer, vacuum integrity, and oxygen control. | Isolation valves, metal hoppers, redundant oxygen monitoring, evacuation and backfill capability, straight-groove O-rings or hygienic seals, and an acceptance leak criterion. ([name redacted]2017gasatomizationequipment pages 21-24) | Useful preventive architecture, but **not evidence that a collector seal failed or overheated**. |
| **Preventive design only** | EURECAT centrifugal atomizer | A sloped lower cone directs particles to a collector at the bottom cap; the chamber is evacuated to about 10⁻³ mbar and backfilled with inert gas. The spinning disk is water- or inert-gas-cooled. | Cooling is selected according to melt temperature; the controlled atmosphere prevents oxidation and contamination. No collector-gasket construction or failure is reported. | Disk cooling, closed metal chamber, vacuum and inert backfill, and gravity-assisted lower-cone collection. (salges2024processingandcharacterization pages 46-50) | No documented collector overheating, glass breakage, seal leak, or oxygen excursion. |
| **Search conclusion** | Published reports, papers, manuals, and specifications located in this search | **No located source confirmed hot shot or molten runoff burning or smoking a powder-collector elastomer seal, thermally shocking and cracking a glass collection vessel or viewport, or raising chamber oxygen specifically through a damaged collector seal.** | The available literature more often reports upstream overheating, outlet plugging, wall deposition, generic seal leakage, or preventive collector design. | Treat proposed heat shields, cooled collector flanges, metal pots, catch trays, and stop rules as engineering recommendations unless a source expressly reports their adoption after such an event. | This evidence gap prevents presenting the requested collector scenarios as documented incidents. |


*Table: This table separates documented atomizer failures from preventive design specifications and identifies how closely each source matches the requested collector-seal, glass-breakage, and oxygen-leak scenarios.*

The clearest nearby failure is the Savannah River Pd-alloy gas-atomization run: erroneous thermocouple readings drove excessive heating, alumina parts fractured, and a broken stopper **blocked** the nozzle. The metal therefore did **not** run into the collector; the reported change was to noncontact infrared pyrometry. The paper’s equipment schematic shows the cooling path and downstream cyclone/collector, but does not depict collector damage. ([name redacted]2020failureanalysisof pages 1-4, [name redacted]2020failureanalysisof pages 4-10, [name redacted]2020failureanalysisof media b6770702)

In Pratt & Whitney’s centrifugal atomizer, the reported disk-drive **oil-seal** leakage must not be mistaken for a leaking powder-collector gasket. Unstable disk-rim operation produced large splats and could clog the outlet; the report calls for shutdown in that condition and describes lower-head blowdown to move retained powder toward the collector. It does not identify a repair for the oil seals. Howmet’s Spraycast-X account likewise reports special seals installed *to avoid* chamber leakage and better cleanliness at low leak-up, without identifying a thermally damaged collector seal. (andrus1989thrustchambermaterial pages 88-91, prichard1992spraycastx"superalloyfor pages 4-6)

## Choosing the hot-side collector, seals and glass

**Separate melt temperature from seal temperature.** For a melt above 1,000 °C, the relevant elastomer limit is the *measured or conservatively predicted temperature at its installed sealing surface*, including credible upset conditions—not the nominal melt temperature or a material name alone. Seal guidance warns that formulation, chemistry, swelling, thermal expansion and gland design all matter; FKM grades are not interchangeable, and even FFKM must be selected by grade and service. A cited mechanical-seal review describes ordinary FKM service around 400 °F (approximately 204 °C), with some specialty *static* compounds rated to 250 °F (approximately 121 °C); these are **not** ratings for direct contact with molten metal. That review is not a collector qualification standard. (huebner2005materialselectionfor pages 5-6, huebner2005materialselectionfor pages 4-5)

**Keep the impact and runoff path metallic and away from elastomers.** The LLNL/Arcast atomizer specification calls for a stainless-steel vacuum chamber, a lower cone, isolation valves and six explosion-rated removable powder hoppers; EURECAT describes a sloped metal lower cone leading to its collector. A separate high-temperature vacuum reactor demonstrates water cooling of a flange and use of Viton seals at *cooled* quartz windows, not at the hot workpiece. Accordingly, a metal receiving pot or catch tray, a shielded or cooled collector flange, and a seal outside any direct shot/runoff path are defensible **design recommendations** to assess and validate—not fixes shown to have followed a collector fire in these publications. Verify their thermal performance and the collector’s pressure/vacuum rating for the actual installation. ([name redacted]2017gasatomizationequipment pages 21-24, jubber1994designofa pages 3-4, salges2024processingandcharacterization pages 46-50)

**Do not substitute an ordinary glass jar for a qualified hot-metal receiver.** In an optical-access high-temperature apparatus, the designers rejected soda-lime and borosilicate glass and selected quartz for its lower thermal expansion and higher continuous operating-temperature capability; they also cushioned and sealed its metal interfaces with gaskets and sized the window for the applicable pressure difference. Comparative glass data give approximate expansion coefficients of 3.4 × 10⁻⁶/°C for borosilicate and 0.55 × 10⁻⁶/°C for fused silica. These properties favor an engineered, protected observation window where optical access is necessary; **neither source certifies quartz or borosilicate as a vessel safe from direct molten-metal impact**. Window strength, mounting stress, thermal gradients and pressure loading still require specific engineering assessment. (angeloni2020designandcommissioning pages 57-63, oikonomopoulou2019materialcompositionsand pages 4-7)

A conservative operating rule is to **stop the melt/atomization sequence and retain the inert atmosphere** if visible runoff, abnormally coarse shot, collector or flange overheating, smoke, glass damage, loss of cooling, a seal leak, or unexplained oxygen rise occurs; keep the collector isolated until the equipment is safe to inspect. This is a proposed stop rule inferred from the documented blocked-outlet/shutdown experience and containment designs, **not** a manufacturer-prescribed rePOWDER procedure. ([name redacted]2017gasatomizationequipment pages 21-24, andrus1989thrustchambermaterial pages 88-91)

## Checking chamber integrity

For a *clean, dry, assembled* chamber—including its collector joints—evacuate, isolate the pump and record pressure against time. The measured gas load is **Q = V(dP/dt)** and contains both leakage and outgassing; a nearly linear sustained rise favors a real leak, whereas a rise that progressively levels off can indicate outgassing/re-adsorption. This test alone does not locate a faulty seal, and a dirty or recently heated chamber can confound it. The published pressure-rise comparison illustrates that distinction. (chung2018vacuumdiagnosisand pages 1-2, santos2005simplevacuumexperiments pages 3-4, chung2018vacuumdiagnosisand pages 2-4, chung2018vacuumdiagnosisand media b1aeea66)

Locate suspect collector flanges and other joints with an appropriately configured **helium leak detector** while applying helium locally. A published large-vessel investigation enclosed individual flange gaps and welds, introduced helium to each enclosure, corrected detector readings for gas diverted through parallel pumping, retightened leaking flanges and re-welded a defective port. Its illustrated enclosure method is useful, but its numerical joint acceptance threshold is specific to that facility. The LLNL/Arcast *atomizer design specification* instead states a whole-system leak requirement of **less than 1 × 10⁻⁶ atm·cm³/s**; the specification does not itself demonstrate that a particular machine passed testing. Set acceptance criteria and test configuration for the actual atomizer rather than transferring either example uncritically. ([name redacted]2017gasatomizationequipment pages 21-24, chung2018vacuumdiagnosisand pages 2-4, chung2018vacuumdiagnosisand pages 4-5, chung2018vacuumdiagnosisand media eee4691c)

## Trace-oxygen indication following loss of power

**No retrieved rePOWDER instruction specifies an automatic post-outage sensor check.** As a documented *analyzer-manual analogy*, the GPR-3100B oxygen analyzer performs power-on diagnostics; its manual describes allowing stabilization and calibration after installation, flushing the selected sample/calibration gas before reading, and ensuring that calibration-gas pressure and temperature are representative of the sample. Its power-failure alarm opens when power is lost. These instructions should not be represented as AMAZEMET settings or as proof that every brief outage invalidates calibration. (analyzer1992ownersmanuala pages 17-21, analyzer1992ownersmanual pages 17-21, analyzer1992ownersmanual pages 11-17)

Before relying on a restarted chamber reading to authorize a new melt, an appropriate **proposed verification** is to confirm analyzer self-test, sample flow and sampling-line integrity; check a low-oxygen reference and a suitable independent span or functional challenge under the installed analyzer manufacturer’s procedure; confirm that alarm and interlock states have returned correctly; and independently confirm chamber pressure integrity and oxygen stability after purge. Do not accept an apparently low displayed oxygen value by itself as evidence that a collector seal is sound. The available oxygen-analyzer manual supports stabilization, controlled sample presentation, zero/span calibration and attention to the power-failure alarm; the LLNL atomizer specification supports redundant oxygen monitoring, but neither supplies a universal atomizer-specific outage acceptance threshold. ([name redacted]2017gasatomizationequipment pages 21-24, analyzer1992ownersmanuala pages 17-21, analyzer1992ownersmanual pages 11-17, analyzer1992ownersmanuala pages 24-29)

| **Documented incident** | SRNL Powder Production Facility, helium gas-spray atomizer, approximately 2.1 kg Pd-alloy charge | Faulty, diverging thermocouple readings prompted excessive RF power. Alumina thermocouple sheaths and the stopper rod failed; the broken rod remained in the nozzle throat and blocked discharge. | Melt temperature was estimated near 1,918–2,060 °C, approaching alumina’s melting point; spring load and slight misalignment probably contributed to creep rupture. | Replace contact thermocouples with non-contact infrared optical pyrometry. The source does **not** report that metal reached or damaged the collector. (pqac-00000032, pqac-00000033) | Adjacent atomizer overheating failure, **not** a collector-seal or glass-vessel incident. |
| **Documented operating problems** | Pratt & Whitney rapid-solidification-rate centrifugal atomizer | Disk-drive oil seals leaked; unstable rim atomization produced large splats that reduced yield or clogged the outlet. Fine powder and detached wall deposits could obstruct flow to the collector can. | Soft copper adhered to chamber walls; deposits could later fall, while unstable atomization and splashing generated coarse material. The oil-seal leak cause was not reported. | Shutdown was required for unstable atomization; lower-head blowdown nozzles were used to assure powder flow. **No oil-seal repair was specified**, so none should be inferred. (pqac-00000034) | Closest documented case involving coarse splats and collector-path blockage, but no burned collector gasket, cracked glass, or oxygen rise. |
| **Reported modification, not a collector incident** | Howmet Spraycast-X vacuum-induction melting and gas-atomization system | Special seal designs were installed to avoid operational leakage after evacuation and argon backfill; low leak-up improved product cleanliness. | High chamber leak-up admitted contaminants and increased oxide and nitride inclusions; very low leak-up limited oxygen and nitrogen pickup during argon processing to generally under 15 ppm. | Improved sealing, evacuation before argon backfill, and operation under tight-vacuum and very-low-leak-up conditions. Collector seals were not identified. (pqac-00000035) | Documents atmosphere-leakage control, **not** hot metal overheating a collector seal. |
| **Preventive specification only** | 2017 LLNL/Arcast free-fall gas atomizer | Stainless-steel high-vacuum chamber; lower cone and six explosion-rated powder-removal hoppers with isolation valves and quick clamps; three redundant paramagnetic oxygen analyzers; specified leak rate below 1 × 10⁻⁶ atm·cm³/s. | Design requirements anticipated reactive, refractory, and radioactive powders and required inert transfer, vacuum integrity, and oxygen control. | Isolation valves, metal hoppers, redundant oxygen monitoring, evacuation and backfill capability, straight-groove O-rings or hygienic seals, and an acceptance leak criterion. (pqac-00000010) | Useful preventive architecture, but **not evidence that a collector seal failed or overheated**. |
| **Preventive design only** | EURECAT centrifugal atomizer | A sloped lower cone directs particles to a collector at the bottom cap; the chamber is evacuated to about 10⁻³ mbar and backfilled with inert gas. The spinning disk is water- or inert-gas-cooled. | Cooling is selected according to melt temperature; the controlled atmosphere prevents oxidation and contamination. No collector-gasket construction or failure is reported. | Disk cooling, closed metal chamber, vacuum and inert backfill, and gravity-assisted lower-cone collection. (pqac-00000045) | No documented collector overheating, glass breakage, seal leak, or oxygen excursion. |
| **Search conclusion** | Published reports, papers, manuals, and specifications located in this search | **No located source confirmed hot shot or molten runoff burning or smoking a powder-collector elastomer seal, thermally shocking and cracking a glass collection vessel or viewport, or raising chamber oxygen specifically through a damaged collector seal.** | The available literature more often reports upstream overheating, outlet plugging, wall deposition, generic seal leakage, or preventive collector design. | Treat proposed heat shields, cooled collector flanges, metal pots, catch trays, and stop rules as engineering recommendations unless a source expressly reports their adoption after such an event. | This evidence gap prevents presenting the requested collector scenarios as documented incidents. |

info.query:
Find reports, manuals, application notes or papers on metal powder atomizers (ultrasonic such as the
AMAZEMET rePOWDER, gas, or centrifugal) and other inert-gas melting equipment in which hot metal,
coarse shot or molten runoff reached the powder collection container or its seals, so that elastomer
seals or gaskets overheated, smoked or burned, glass collection vessels or view ports cracked from
thermal shock, or the atmosphere's oxygen rose because a collector seal leaked. For each give the
equipment, what happened, the cause found and the fix (for example seal material, heat shields,
cooled flanges, metal collection pots, catch trays, interlocks or stop rules). Also report published
guidance on choosing seals and glass for powder collectors under melts above 1000 C, on leak testing
(rate of rise, helium) of atomizer chambers, and on how trace-oxygen sensors on such chambers should
be checked after a power failure.
